content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines in 2018 regarding the use, adaptation, and redistribution of their work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations of the work must be licensed under the same or equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, a disclaimer must be included stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. Disputes arising under the license are to be mediated according to the rules of the World Intellectual Property Organization. The WHO last issued guidance on aircraft disinsection in 1995, but this guidance has since become outdated. The rapid spread of mosquito-borne diseases, such as Zika virus, has highlighted the need for updated recommendations. The objectives of a recent consultation included reviewing challenges faced by end-users of disinsection products, evaluating current and new procedures, assessing the need for new insecticide formulations, and making recommendations on disinsection methods. The International Health Regulations (IHR), adopted in 2005 and enforced in 2007, define disinsection as the process of controlling or killing insect vectors of human disease in baggage, cargo, containers, conveyances, goods, and postal parcels. The IHR emphasizes that disinsection should avoid injury and minimize discomfort to individuals. In 2016, WHO convened an expert group in response to the Zika virus outbreak, which found that the effectiveness of disinsection in preventing pathogen importation was low compared to the risk posed by infected travelers. Currently, WHO recommends specific insecticides for aircraft disinsection, including permethrin, d-phenothrin, and 1-R-trans-phenothrin in various formulations. These insecticides must comply with WHO specifications and the regulations of the destination country. WHO-recommended disinsection methods include block-away aerosol application, pre-flight aerosol application, top-of-descent spraying, and residual insecticide treatment. Each method has specific protocols to ensure efficacy and safety. Residual insecticide treatments are part of routine pest control measures, primarily for cockroach control. These treatments involve spraying internal surfaces of the aircraft, excluding food preparation areas, with professional pest control operators using WHO-specified equipment. The frequency of retreatment depends on cleaning schedules, and areas undergoing substantial cleaning may require supplementary touch-up spraying. In sensitive areas, aerosol application may be necessary instead of compression sprayers. Challenges in aircraft disinsection include pyrethroid resistance in mosquitoes and regulatory restrictions in some countries against certain products. Consequently, new products and non-chemical methods are needed. Collaboration with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) is essential to develop improved practices. New Zealand, which lacks vector species targeted by disinsection, enforces strict biosecurity measures under its Biosecurity Act of 1993 and Health Act of 1956. New Zealand and Australia have jointly developed disinsection procedures based on WHO recommendations, including pre-embarkation spraying methods. These methods aim to eliminate invertebrates present at the time of treatment and provide residual protection against those entering the cabin before departure. The importance of engaging qualified pest control operators, training cabin crew, and treating baggage and cargo areas was emphasized. Frequent cleaning of certain cabin areas reduces the effectiveness of residual treatments, necessitating reapplication. Resistance to pyrethroid insecticides among mosquito vectors is increasing, and regulatory restrictions in some regions further complicate disinsection efforts. New products and methods, including non-chemical approaches, are required to address these challenges effectively.
